title: Anahat Singh Becomes First Indian to Win World Junior Squash Championship, Ending Egypt's 15-Year Reign
excerpt: The 18-year-old from Delhi defeated Egypt's Ruqayya Salem in straight games to clinch India's maiden individual world junior title in squash, breaking a 21-year jinx she once called a 'curse.'
body:
• Anahat Singh, 18, won the 2026 World Junior Squash Championship in Ontario, Canada — the first Indian ever to win the individual title
  • She defeated Egypt's second-seeded Ruqayya Salem 11-3, 11-7, 11-9 in the final, ending Egypt's 15-year stranglehold on the girls' title
  • Singh is the first Indian to reach the final since Joshna Chinappa in 2005 and the first non-Egyptian champion since Amanda Sobhy in 2010
  • The World No. 20, coached by French legends Stéphane Galifi and Grégory Gaultier, called it a dream come true in her last year as a junior

Breaking a 'Curse' on the Biggest Stage

Anahat Singh had played in four World Junior Squash Championships. She had lost in the quarter-finals. She had lost in the semi-finals. She had called the tournament a curse. On Saturday, in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ontario, she broke it.

https://x.com/Media_SAI/status/2081089126204678557

The 18-year-old from Delhi demolished Egypt's Ruqayya Salem 11-3, 11-7, 11-9 in the girls' singles final to become the first Indian ever to win the World Junior Squash Championship. It was a clinical, composed performance — the kind that announces not just a winner, but an arrival.

"I still feel like I'm dreaming. I've always said, 'This tournament's a curse.' This is my last year as a junior and my only chance to win it. It means the world."

— Anahat Singh, 2026 World Junior Squash Champion

Dismantling Egyptian Dominance

Egyptian players had won every girls' title at the World Junior Championship since 2011 — a 15-year stranglehold on the tournament that had become one of squash's defining narratives. Singh did not just break the streak; she did it by beating four Egyptian players across six matches, dropping only two games in the entire tournament.

In the quarter-finals, she overcame Habiba Rizk 3-1. In the semi-finals, she dispatched Barb Sameh 3-1 with a display of defensive resilience and precise shot selection. And in the final, Salem — the second seed who had fought her way through her own side of the draw — was allowed just 19 points across three games.

Singh is the first non-Egyptian champion since Amanda Sobhy of the United States won the title in 2010. Before Singh, India's best result was Joshna Chinappa's runner-up finish in 2005 and Dipika Pallikal's bronze in 2010.

The Making of a Champion

Singh's rise has been one of the fastest in Asian squash history. Ranked No. 20 in the world — the youngest Asian ever to break into the top 20, surpassing Malaysian legend Nicol David's record — she has assembled a coaching team that reads like a squash hall of fame: French coaches Stéphane Galifi and Grégory Gaultier, with Indian squash icon Saurav Ghosal serving as her mentor.

This season alone, she won the Squash on Fire Open (her first bronze-level title on the professional tour), defended her Indian Open crown and became the World Junior No. 1. Last year, she was part of the Indian team that won the Squash World Cup — the country's first team world title.

Cyrus Poncha, secretary-general of the Squash Rackets Federation of India, called the moment a culmination of years of institutional effort. "It's a historic moment for Indian squash," he said. "The late Mr N Ramachandran, SRFI patron and visionary of the Indian Squash Academy, always said it was his dream that India produce a world champion in individual events. We achieved it in doubles, but to replicate that success in singles — it is really a dream come true."

What Comes Next

With her junior career now complete, Singh's focus shifts entirely to the professional tour. Her top-20 ranking makes her a legitimate contender at major events, and her age — still just 18 — suggests the best is ahead of her. The senior World Championships and the Asian Games loom as the next major targets.

For Indian squash, the win signals a generational shift. The sport, long overshadowed by cricket and increasingly by badminton and wrestling, now has a genuine global star. Sports Minister Dr Mansukh Mandaviya was among the first to congratulate Singh, reflecting the growing institutional recognition of squash in India.
